steps.text:
### Adding MIG (Multi‑Instance GPU) Partitioning to Your Existing GPU Servers Below is a practical checklist of what you’ll need to do to enable MIG on the GPUs in your fleet. The steps assume you are using NVIDIA‑based GPUs that support MIG (e.g., A100, H100, or newer). If any of your servers have older GPUs (e.g., V100, T4, RTX {{int:24:36}}‑series) you’ll need to replace those cards because they do **not** support MIG. | Area | What you need / what to do | Why it matters | |------|----------------------------|----------------| | **Hardware** | • Verify each GPU model supports MIG (A100, H100, A30, etc.).
• Ensure the server’s power supply, cooling, and chassis can handle the additional thermal load of multiple instances running concurrently. | MIG is a hardware‑level feature; unsupported GPUs cannot be partitioned. | | **Firmware / BIOS** | • Update the GPU firmware to the latest NVIDIA version.
• If the server’s BIOS has any GPU‑related settings (e.g., “Above‑4G decoding”, “PCIe link speed”), set them to the recommended values for your GPU model. | Firmware updates contain MIG‑related bug fixes and enable the feature. | | **Driver** | • Install the NVIDIA driver version that includes MIG support (≥ {{int:368:552}}.xx for A100, ≥ {{int:420:630}}.xx for newer GPUs).
• Verify the driver is correctly loaded (`nvidia-smi` should show “MIG Mode”). | The driver provides the user‑space tools (`nvidia‑smi`) needed to enable/disable MIG and to create instances. | | **CUDA Toolkit** | • Use a CUDA version that matches the driver (e.g., CUDA 11.4+ for A100).
• Re‑compile any GPU‑accelerated applications if they depend on a specific CUDA version. | Applications must be built against a compatible CUDA runtime to see the MIG‑exposed devices. | | **Operating System** | • Recent Linux distributions (RHEL 8/9, Ubuntu 20.04/22.04, Rocky 8/9) are recommended.
• Ensure the kernel supports the NVIDIA driver (most modern kernels do). | A supported OS avoids driver‑kernel incompatibilities. | | **Enabling MIG** | 1. **Check current mode**: `nvidia-smi -L` (shows each GPU).
2. **Enable MIG** (if not already): `sudo nvidia-smi -i -mig 1`.
3. **Create instances**: `sudo nvidia-smi mig -cgi ` (e.g., `1g.5gb` for a 1‑GPU‑instance with 5 GB memory).
4. **Verify**: `nvidia-smi -L` now lists MIG instances as separate devices. | MIG must be explicitly turned on per GPU; then you allocate the desired number and size of instances. | | **Kubernetes / Container Orchestration** | • Install the NVIDIA GPU Operator (or the older Device Plugin) that supports MIG.
• Define `resource` requests in pod specs using the MIG‑specific device IDs (e.g., `nvidia.com/gpu: 1` with `nvidia.com/mig-profile: 1g.5gb`).
• Optionally, use **NVIDIA MIG Manager** to dynamically provision instances based on workload. | The operator will expose each MIG instance as a separate device to the scheduler, allowing pods to request the exact partition they need. | | **Monitoring & Management** | • Use **DCGM** (Data Center GPU Manager) or **nvidia‑smi** for health checks.
• Integrate with Prometheus/Grafana dashboards to watch per‑instance utilization, temperature, and errors. | MIG adds more granular devices; you’ll want visibility per instance to avoid overload. | | **Licensing / Software** | • No extra NVIDIA driver license is required for MIG, but some enterprise features (e.g., NVIDIA AI Enterprise, NVIDIA Fleet Command) may need a subscription if you use them. | Be aware of any software that might have additional licensing constraints. | | **Testing / Validation** | • After enabling MIG, run a small benchmark or inference job on each instance to confirm performance and isolation.
• Verify that existing non‑MIG workloads continue to run (they will see the full GPU unless you explicitly migrate them). | Guarantees that the change didn’t break existing services. | | **Documentation & SOPs** | • Document the chosen MIG profiles per workload (e.g., 2g.10gb for training, 1g.5gb for inference).
• Create a standard operating procedure for adding/removing MIG instances when capacity changes. | Consistency helps the ops team manage the fleet without ad‑hoc changes. | --- #### Example Workflow (single GPU) ```bash # 1. Verify driver & GPU support nvidia-smi # 2. Enable MIG on GPU 0 sudo nvidia-smi -i 0 -mig 1 # 3. Create two 1‑GPU‑instance partitions (1g.5gb each) sudo nvidia-smi mig -i 0 -cgi 1g.5gb -C # 4. List the new instances nvidia-smi -L # Output will show: # GPU 0 (UUID: ...) MIG 1g.5gb (UUID: ...) # GPU 0 (UUID: ...) MIG 1g.5gb (UUID: ...) ``` After the above, the Kubernetes GPU Operator will automatically discover the new MIG devices and make them schedulable. --- ### Rough Timeline & Effort Estimate | Phase | Effort (person‑days) | Comments | |-------|---------------------|----------| | **Discovery** (inventory, firmware version check) | 1‑2 | Use existing inventory (the CSV you exported) to flag which servers need GPU upgrades. | | **Pilot** (one rack or 2‑3 servers) | 2‑3 | Enable MIG, test a workload, verify monitoring. | | **Roll‑out** (full fleet) | 0.5‑1 day per {{int:16:24}} servers (parallelized) | With scripting (Ansible, Salt, etc.) you can push drivers, enable MIG, and create instances en‑masse. | | **Kubernetes integration** | 1‑2 days | Install/upgrade NVIDIA GPU Operator, adjust pod specs. | | **Documentation & Training** | 1 day | Write SOPs and brief the ops team. | *Overall, a small to medium‑size environment (≤ {{int:16:24}} GPUs) can be fully MIG‑enabled in about 1‑2 weeks of coordinated effort.* --- ### Bottom Line - **Check hardware compatibility** – only A100/H100/A30 (and newer) support MIG. - **Update firmware & drivers** to the latest versions. - **Enable MIG** per GPU via `nvidia‑smi`, then create the desired partitions. - **Integrate with Kubernetes** using the NVIDIA GPU Operator so workloads can request specific MIG profiles. - **Monitor** each instance and document the configuration for future scaling. If you’d like help generating the exact `nvidia‑smi` commands for each server (based on the CSV you have) or need a script to automate the rollout, just let me know!
